dimensions.name: Sales impact
dimensions.description: Does the section make an evaluator want to hire Jacobs? Three to five win themes are named once and threaded as headings, callout titles, and closers; every section opens on the client's situation and closes on the client's future with a named lead and three outcomes; a skimmer reading only headings, bold, and sidebars gets the whole case (voice-guide Rules 11, 13, 26, 27).

anchors.3: Reads as a compliance response. Headings are RFP labels or bare project names, themes are stated once or not at all, sections end on legal boilerplate, a table, or a placeholder. The evaluator finishes knowing what Jacobs is, not what the client gains. (The Richmond pilot: 0 benefit headings, 0 themes threaded, closes on litigation text and a placeholder.)
anchors.6: Themes are present and most headings carry a benefit noun. Most sections close on a benefit paragraph, but a feature list, a hedge, or a legal paragraph sits in the closing slot somewhere, and at least one theme never recurs as a heading.
anchors.9: Three to five themes recur verbatim as headings, callout titles, and closers, each at least three times across cover letter, executive summary, and section headings. Every section opens on the client and ends with a 40-70-word next-chapter paragraph naming the client, the lead person or team, and three outcomes. The bottom line is unmistakable from headings and bold alone, as in Hull's 'Your next chapter' and Santa Monica's 'Bottom line'.

dimensions.name: Proof density
dimensions.description: Numbers, names, dates, and named tools per 100 words, delivered in four registers (inline figure, stat callout or exhibit pointed to in bold, table row, named and titled third-party voice), with no more than three numeric facts per sentence and every paragraph unshippable to a competitor (Rules 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 25).

anchors.3: Fewer than 4 numbers per 100 words, or numbers stacked five or more to a sentence. One register only (all tables or all prose). No named people with credentials, no named tools, no client identifiers; paragraphs a competitor could paste unchanged. References are key-value tables without a quantified accomplishment.
anchors.6: 4-4.5 numbers per 100 words in two or three registers. Most claims carry a figure and most subsections have one unshippable item, but a few paragraphs are generic, at least one sentence stacks more than five facts, and there is no named, titled third-party voice.
anchors.9: 4.5-6.5 numbers per 100 words (Hull 5.66, Santa Monica 5.47) with at most three per sentence outside facility-scoping sentences. All four registers appear within any two consecutive pages. Every paragraph carries a proper noun, a number, or a named action; each subsection holds two or more of named person with credential, named tool, client identifier, quantified offer; every reference has three relevance tags and a dollar or percent result; at least one named, titled quote or client-attributed figure per major section.

dimensions.name: Consequence linkage
dimensions.description: Every performance figure is tied to a comparator (RFP threshold, industry range, client scale, prior state) and to a client consequence in the same sentence; bold text reads as a chain of outcomes; paragraphs end on what the client gains; proof exhibits end in the client's outcome column; value-adds carry a dollar value (Rules 12, 13, 19, 33).

anchors.3: Figures float without a comparator (TRIR, EMR, D&B rating, portfolio counts stated bare). Consequences are quarantined in a 'Why this matters' block or absent. Bold marks topics. Tables end in feature columns. Value-adds commit to a cadence with no value attached.
anchors.6: Most headline figures carry a comparator. Roughly a third of paragraphs end on a benefit clause; some bold marks outcomes; some exhibits have a value column; some value-adds are quantified.
anchors.9: Every performance figure has its comparator inside the sentence ('EMR of 0.45, well below the RFP requirement of 1.0'). At least 35% of paragraphs end on a bolded two- or three-outcome clause; reading only the bold text yields client outcomes; 70% or more of bold runs contain a number, a client noun, or an outcome verb; every proof exhibit's rightmost column names the client's outcome; every value-add carries a dollar value or measurable quantity summed to one headline.

dimensions.name: Voice and rhythm
dimensions.description: Sentence and paragraph cadence in the winners' band: median 18-25 words, p90 at or under 40, none over 50 outside boilerplate; paragraphs of one or two sentences averaging 30-45 words; verb-bearing punch sentences at paragraph edges paired with a long sentence; closing triads with the serial comma; punctuation inside budget; actor-first openers; no aphorisms or meta-narration (Rules 1-6).

anchors.3: p90 above 45 or paragraphs averaging more than 60 words. Punch sentences are bold run-in labels without verbs. Colon-and-semicolon stacks, em-dash asides, aphorisms, meta-narration. Fewer than 2 triads per 1,000 words, or triads without the serial comma. (The pilot: p90 60, 63.7-word paragraphs, 13 verbless run-ins, 15.8 colons and 10.7 semicolons per 1,000 words, 0.5 triads.)
anchors.6: Median in band but p90 near 40 and some paragraphs over 100 words. Punch sentences exist but sit mid-paragraph or lack a verb. Occasional stacked punctuation; a few triads; under 20% actor-first openers.
anchors.9: Median 18-25 (aim 20-24), p90 at or under 38, no sentence over 50. Paragraphs average 30-45 words, at least 55% one or two sentences, none over 110. A long-short pair opens and closes every section. At least 8 triads per 1,000 words with the serial comma; colons at or under 6, semicolons at or under 4, em dashes at or under 9 per 1,000 words; at least 30% actor-first openers; zero aphorisms and zero meta-narration.

dimensions.name: Client specificity
dimensions.description: The client opens every section as grammatical subject and sits in the beneficiary slot of Jacobs sentences; the client's own vocabulary (permits, orders, systems, place names) is used; needs are framed as aspirations or operating conditions; 'you/your' is spent on collaboration and respect only; commitments carry a named owner, 'will', an operational verb, and a cadence (Rules 20-25).

anchors.3: Client framed as buyer ('gets', 'is buying', 'counterparty', 'balance sheet'). Deficits catalogued in Qualifications. Generic paragraphs. 'You' mixed into third-person paragraphs or used in sentences about shortcomings. Jacobs called 'the operator' or 'they'. Commitments in present tense with no owner.
anchors.6: Client opens most sections and is named in about 40% of paragraphs. Some client vocabulary; a few generic passages; needs mostly framed as aspirations; occasional buyer or deficit wording; most commitments have an owner and 'will'.
anchors.9: Every H2 opens with the client's situation, Jacobs absent from sentence one. At least 40% of paragraphs name the client (Hull 0.44, Santa Monica 0.40), always as beneficiary. Client identifiers appear in the client's terms. Every 'you/your' sentence names something the client owns, values, or will receive. Every commitment reads [named person or role] will [operational verb] [object] [cadence]. Every subsection holds two or more unshippable items.

dimensions.name: Structure and scannability
dimensions.description: Heading density and content, bold purpose, paragraph size, exhibit pointers, and device discipline: a reader who skims headings, bold, sidebars, and table headers gets the argument in order (Rules 7-11, 32, 33).

anchors.3: More than 220 or fewer than 100 words per heading. Numbered RFP-echo headings without benefit nouns; bare project names as headings. Run-in bold used as the section skeleton. No exhibit pointers. Reference projects as key-value tables. Skimmer sees topics, not outcomes. (The pilot: 281 words per heading, 0 benefit headings, 13 run-ins as spine.)
anchors.6: Headings every 100-220 words with mixed benefit content. Bold partly on outcomes. Exhibits present but not pointed to from prose. Some run-ins longer than six words; bullets mostly parallel; at most one device misused per section.
anchors.9: A heading every 130-180 words (Hull 149, Santa Monica 158), each a 3-9-word benefit noun phrase in sentence case, at least one per section naming the client or its state, at most one assertion heading per section, no unmandated digits. Bold 10-30 runs per 1,000 words with at least 70% on outcomes. About every third paragraph points to an exhibit. Bullets 3-8 parallel items with lead-ins of six words or fewer. Every device matches the Rule 32 table and repeats a claim the prose already made.

dimensions.name: Incumbent and concession handling
dimensions.description: Competition is never named; the incumbent's shortcomings are stated as the client's aspirations; required negatives follow the four-move concession (scale, bound, resolve, no impact) with a resolution column; nothing negative is volunteered beyond the RFP ask; weaknesses are acknowledged in a subordinate clause and answered in the main clause (Rules 28-31).

anchors.3: Competitor named. Client, staff, or program blamed. Negative tables or admissions volunteered. Self-disclaimers about our own evidence ('We make no claim yet'). Concessions end on a warning, a hedge, or an aphorism. (The pilot: incumbent named six times, a volunteered incident table, an ownership-model swipe, a violations paragraph closing on 'A firm that discloses a $660 fine will disclose a permit exceedance.')
anchors.6: Competitor unnamed. Some deficit language survives. RFP-required disclosures made with a resolution but missing scale context or the no-impact close. One concession runs longer than a sentence.
anchors.9: Zero competitor names; 'the previous contract operator' or 'traditional O&M providers' throughout. Incumbent gaps written as what the client is seeking. Every disclosed negative follows scale, bound, resolve, no impact in one paragraph, with a resolution column in any table. No volunteered negatives. Each weakness is one sentence: subordinate acknowledgement, main-clause answer on the evaluator's criterion, as in Hull's EPA Region 1 reference sentence.

dimensions.name: Holistic top-writer judgment
dimensions.description: Would the author of the Hull or Santa Monica sections sign this as their own? One voice throughout, confident without hype, brand mechanics correct, nothing for a senior editor to fix before layout, zero editorial residue in the body (Rules 34, 35 and the whole).

anchors.3: A copy editor would rewrite most paragraphs. Tags, hedges, meta-narration, and aphorisms show the writer's process. The reader sees the seams between sources ('$12 billion [VERIFY — a second source states more than $15 billion]'). Banned words present.
anchors.6: Competent and clean with no disqualifying fault. A senior editor would tighten 20-30% of sentences, re-head several subsections, and restore a few serial commas before release.
anchors.9: Indistinguishable from the winning sections. A senior editor changes fewer than one sentence in ten. The body carries no brackets, notes, or hedges; conflicting figures were settled in the fact pack and the prose shows one number at a precision both sources support. Brand mechanics (sentence-case headings, spaced em dash, en-dash ranges, serial comma, 'Jacobs' possessive) are correct throughout. Every paragraph earns its place in the client's decision.

pass_rule: every dimension ≥8 and mean ≥8.5 and all hard gates
